item.text: I’ll record your corrections and permissions, then develop three concepts grounded in your work. I’ll omit the near-miss story, exclude the whiteboard photo, and attribute the scanning improvement to the ward team.

item.aggregated_output:
# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does any sentence in it say more than the fact sheet does: a ranking, a reason, which came first, how a thing was left, a day, a place? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.
# Asking

## Facts

At the first stop your questions go in one message, numbered. `reading-a-profile.md` says what they are.

## A choice

Where you offer a choice, the concept above all, give the ones you would not choose as fully as the one you would. Then say which you would choose, and why.

If the person tells you to choose, choose. Write what you chose, and what you chose it over, into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.

## If the person will not answer

Some people will not answer your questions, or will say: decide everything. Then:

- **What is a matter of taste, you decide:** the concept, the look, the order. Say which you chose and what you chose it over.
- **A fact, you do not decide.** What you could not confirm stays off the page. A figure whose meaning you do not know, a project you cannot say ever ran, a paper you cannot say they wrote, a title you cannot say is theirs: leave it out, or carry it in the script marked "to confirm", and stand nothing on it. Build the concept on the facts that needed no confirming. The person's own resume is no exception: if you asked whether a project ever ran and they did not say, "real-time system" is still not confirmed, and it is not printed.
- **Say what is waiting on them,** as a numbered list at the top of what you hand over.

A wrong guess about someone's taste costs them an afternoon. A wrong claim about their work is read by the people they most want to convince, and it is their name on the site, not yours.

# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

item.text: ISBAR is the strongest direction: it is a form you use every day, and you led a team that redesigned it. I’ll use its five parts to organize the page, with five document panels carrying the work through the scroll. The mobile version will keep the same story in a readable sequence with lighter motion.

from pathlib import Path
p=Path('docs/story')
f=p/'facts.md'
s=f.read_text().replace('Status: material read; awaiting Aoife\\'s confirmation.', 'Status: material read; Aoife supplied corrections and delegated remaining design decisions.').replace('No answers or approvals received yet.', 'Answers received below. Earlier pending items remain unresolved unless explicitly answered; the confirmations below supersede conflicting source claims.')
s+='''

## Confirmed answers — second user message

These identifiers are the source references for the concept and storyboard. All come directly from Aoife's second message.

- F01: The near-miss story is true. No bed number, initial or drug may appear; omit if it cannot be told safely. Decision: omit the story entirely.
- F02: Whiteboard photograph contains patient initials and bed numbers and cannot be shown. Excluded, including blurred/cropped versions.
- F03: Empty handover sheets may be shown. Filled examples are not authorized. Actual blank files have not yet been supplied.
- F04: 71% to 94% was a ward result involving pharmacy, IT, night staff and Aoife. Her contribution was forty hours of observation, identifying three workarounds, and getting scanners moved to the medication room door. Exact measurement definition, dates and denominator remain unanswered.
- F05: Formal titles: CNM1 and Nursing Informatics Link Nurse, one day per week. Do not use Clinical Informatics Lead as a job title.
- F06: Hospital may be named; hospital logo may not be used. Hospital identity is sourced from material/linkedin.md.
- F07: Aoife led a group of five on the handover sheet. The form is ISBAR: identify, situation, background, assessment, recommendation. She describes it as familiar to nurses in Ireland. Do not turn that into a universal knowledge claim in site copy.
- F08: Audience: hiring for clinical informatics jobs in hospitals and companies selling them systems. Goal: work in clinical informatics full time from 2026. This is an aspiration, not a claim that she has already moved roles.
- F09: Daily working forms: ISBAR handover, early warning score chart, care plan and audit cycle (plan, do, study, act).
- F10: For unanswered matters, Aoife asks us to use judgment and disclose assumptions. This delegates design choices, not the invention of facts or permissions.

## Still unresolved; exclude or hold from public copy

- Exact scan-measure definition, period and measurement method; the numerical outcome will stay out of publication-ready text until specified. Ward attribution is confirmed.
- Six-ward adoption/current use, preceptorship count/period, actual dashboard use and personal contribution, research interview count/authorship/presentation/reuse permissions, MSc completion and current duration claims.
- Permission for any other employer artifacts, quotes, patient/client stories or colleague images. Nothing further is inferred.
- Verified contact address, approved CV, existing website/domain and actual blank handover files.
- Formative influences and additional responsibilities in the nursing roles. No origin anecdote or invented duties will fill these gaps.
'''
f.write_text(s)
(p/'concepts.md').write_text('''# Three concepts and selection

## Trade forms considered

ISBAR handover, early warning score chart, care plan, PDSA audit cycle (all confirmed daily forms, F09), and medication administration record (a trade form, not confirmed as Aoife's daily tool). Choose from the confirmed forms.

## 1. The handover — selected

- Question: How can nursing experience make clinical systems work better on a ward?
- Form: ISBAR in its established order. Identify opens with Aoife and her role; Situation establishes the current career direction; Background carries career context and handover work; Assessment shows the observation and workaround study; Recommendation brings together actions, evidence and contact.
- Object: five paper panels, one for each ISBAR field, assembled as one handover document at rest. These are an authored portfolio device, not a purported hospital form. Approved empty sheets can later provide authentic evidence separately.
- Transformations: Identify assembles the five fields into a legible sheet; Background separates them to expose the group-of-five handover contribution; Assessment makes a diagram of observations and workarounds; Recommendation reassembles the full document with evidence and contact.
- Opening: panels arrange from the ISBAR working form Aoife says she uses daily. No invented career origin story. Close: the document becomes whole, offering the confirmed nursing/observation/change experience to clinical informatics employers.
- Grounding: F03–F09; sourced role dates in facts.md, subject to final factual review.
- Needs: blank sheets for any genuine before/after exhibit; contact/CV; metric definition if figures are included. No dependency on prohibited photo or logo.
- Why hers: the five-field form carries the specific handover redesign she led and the specific observation-to-scanner-location work she performed.

## 2. The improvement cycle

- Question: How do you turn a ward workaround into a system change?
- Form: Plan, Do, Study, Act, then Plan for the next cycle. Chapters hold career direction/context; observation method; workaround findings; scanner move/team contribution; future role/contact respectively.
- Object: eight paper audit cards, two per stage, forming a working audit packet. A designed evidence packet, not an existing artifact claimed to be Aoife's.
- Transformations: Plan pairs question/evidence cards; Study aligns observed patterns with possible interventions; Act assembles confirmed contribution and attributed ward outcome. Same cards remain throughout.
- Opening: packet organized into the daily PDSA cycle (F09). Close: next Plan opens toward full-time clinical informatics.
- Grounding: F04, F05, F08, F09. Other interventions from the abstract remain excluded until attribution/reuse is clear.
- Needs: contact/CV and scan metric definition; permission before displaying research source material.
- Why hers: it follows her forty hours of observation and the scanner relocation rather than a generic improvement slogan.
- Tradeoff: strongest for the scanning work, but the repeated Plan and handover project fit less naturally than ISBAR.

## 3. The care plan

- Question: What should a clinical system help a nurse do?
- Form: a proposed care-plan structure, Assessment, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation, Review. These are editorial planning stages, not a claim about her hospital's exact care-plan headings. Holds identity/context; target role; handover redesign; observed workarounds and change; future work/contact.
- Object: six bound paper leaves making a care-plan booklet. Portfolio text replaces patient fields; no patient example is invented.
- Transformations: Assessment opens the booklet to identity/context; Implementation pairs leaves around the five-person handover work; Evaluation places observation and action leaves together; Review closes into a complete professional evidence booklet.
- Opening: a booklet drawn from the care plan she uses daily (F09). Close: a review of confirmed professional contribution and contact.
- Grounding: F03–F09.
- Needs: exact care-plan headings before committing to an authentic clinical form, blank sheet assets, contact/CV. No employer care-plan artifact assumed available.
- Why hers: its pages carry her specific handover and workaround work, rather than simulated patient care.
- Tradeoff: risks confusing a professional portfolio with a patient care plan; lacks ISBAR's confirmed headings.

## Selection

Aoife delegated unanswered design choices in F10. Choose concept 1, The handover, over the audit cycle and care plan. ISBAR has confirmed headings, ties directly to the redesign she led and supports both clinical and vendor hiring audiences without imitating a patient record. No separate concept approval requested because choosing was delegated. Storyboard approval remains pending.

## Tests

All three are continuous sequences with one persistent document object, not changing visual metaphors. Content stays accessible outside 3D. The primary concept loses the document's structural relationships when the scene is removed; static equivalents must preserve them. No stethoscope, hospital logo or patient data. Each first screen must expose name, formal role, one confirmed contribution and contact navigation. No inference that Aoife alone caused the ward result.
''')
(p/'decided-for-you.md').write_text('''# Decisions delegated by Aoife

Aoife asked us to use judgment for unanswered matters and disclose assumptions (F10). Facts and publication permissions are not assumed.

| Decision | Why | How to change |
|---|---|---|
| Choose ISBAR over PDSA and care plan | Confirmed headings and direct link to the redesign she led | Choose either alternative in concepts.md |
| Omit the near-miss story entirely | It is unnecessary to explain her contribution and Aoife explicitly permits omission | Only revisit with a separately approved safe account |
| Exclude whiteboard photo and hospital logo | Explicit user restrictions | Do not revisit without new explicit authorization |
| Treat five panels as designed portfolio documents | Gives 3D a content-bearing role without fabricating an employer artifact | Replace surface references with approved blank sheets when supplied |
| Use professional hiring contact as the final action | F08 specifies clinical informatics hiring audience | Change CTA destination once contact preference is supplied |
| Keep unconfirmed counts, scan definition, qualifications and assets out of final copy | Design delegation does not establish facts | Supply exact details/permissions |
| Default to warm paper, dark ink and teal | Derived from the document object; readable and suited to clinical work | Choose another palette in storyboard.md |
| English-only, no blog/chat/testimonials at launch | Evidence-focused hiring site; no source material for the extras | Add verified content and change scope |
| Static HTML content with optional 3D enhancement | Readability and access must survive devices and motion preferences | Keep this baseline; motion intensity can change |
| Assume one public landing page and optional project detail views | Current confirmed material supports a focused sequence | Expand when approved evidence exists |

Not assumed: MSc completion, an existing website, a verified email, exact scan measure, sole authorship of poster, six-ward adoption or permission for additional employer materials.
''')
PY"

First viewport: name, both formal titles, one-day remit, hiring direction, and proof that Aoife led a five-person ISBAR redesign. Persistent Contact and CV access (CV only when ready). ## Phone and fallback behavior

| Condition | Experience |
|---|---|
| Phone | Single column; small static/finitely animated document above each text section. Same five panels rearrange briefly on section entry, no long pinning or horizontal swipes. | Reduced motion | Static five-field illustrations per chapter; no camera travel, parallax or transition. Full content and navigation identical |
| No WebGL | Static SVG/HTML document diagrams show the same evidence relationships |
| No JavaScript | Server-rendered or pre-rendered HTML, native anchors, static diagrams, actual contact/CV links; all evidence remains available |

Logical headings, skip link, visible keyboard focus, contrast checks, alt text and keyboard-operable detail views. No critical text solely in a texture; no scroll-controlled focus. Desktop camera keeps faces readable rather than spinning the document.

Recommended: warm paper background #F4F1E9, ink #172A2D, accent teal #006B64; panels #FFFEF8 with thin charcoal rules, tiny registration labels and restrained shadows. Accent indicates chapter/progress/links rather than medical severity. No red alerts or faux patient monitors.

Alternatives for later visual review: cool chart paper (#EDF3F4 ground, #14292E ink, #245F82 accent, white matte panels); night desk (#142429 ground, #F1F2EB ink, #78C6B8 accent, pale paper panels). These are styling options for the same concept, not additional concepts. Warm paper is selected under delegated judgment; do not add a palette switch to the public site.

Two typefaces: Source Sans 3 for navigation/body text; IBM Plex Sans for form headings and panel printing. Both have a practical document character. Self-host licensed font files with system sans fallbacks. Desktop titles roughly 48–72px, phone 32–40px; body 18px desktop/16–18px phone; line length about 60–70 characters. Further implementation requirements: descriptive page title and metadata, readable social preview, canonical URL after domain choice, optimized image sizes, lazy-loaded 3D after HTML, simple low-poly panels and capped rendering resolution. Target LCP ≤2.5s, CLS ≤0.1 and INP ≤200ms, then validate on a mid-range phone; these are future acceptance targets, not measured results. No third-party analytics assumed. Test keyboard access, reduced motion and JS/WebGL fallbacks before launch. Do not include patient material in bundles or hidden assets.

| 5.2 | 1 | Complete handover document, stationary for reading | Confirmed contribution summary; target role; contact/CV | None | Next role and contact — F05, F07, F08; destination pending. No fabricated recommendation/testimonial |

Desktop total: approximately 10 screens. Compress any transition that does not introduce evidence; never require visitors to finish the sequence to contact Aoife. Final copy is a later editorial step; no polished captions invented here.

## Thirty-second visitor

First viewport: name, both formal titles, one-day remit, hiring direction, and proof that Aoife led a five-person ISBAR redesign. Persistent Contact and CV access (CV only when ready). Five-item chapter rail with full names plus a skip-to-evidence link. 3D never delays first content; no loading gate or opening film.

## Phone and fallback behavior

| Condition | Experience |
|---|---|
| Phone | Single column; small static/finitely animated document above each text section. Same five panels rearrange briefly on section entry, no long pinning or horizontal swipes. Compact chapter menu; contact always easy to find. Evidence images open as readable images with descriptive text. Target 44px touch controls and at least 16px body text. Scene can be disabled on weaker devices |
| Reduced motion | Static five-field illustrations per chapter; no camera travel, parallax or transition. Full content and navigation identical |
| No WebGL | Static SVG/HTML document diagrams show the same evidence relationships |
| No JavaScript | Server-rendered or pre-rendered HTML, native anchors, static diagrams, actual contact/CV links; all evidence remains available |

WebGL is an enhancement. Scene faces are visual duplicates of accessible HTML, hidden from assistive technology. Logical headings, skip link, visible keyboard focus, contrast checks, alt text and keyboard-operable detail views. No critical text solely in a texture; no scroll-controlled focus. Desktop camera keeps faces readable rather than spinning the document.

## Look and type

Recommended: warm paper background #F4F1E9, ink #172A2D, accent teal #006B64; panels #FFFEF8 with thin charcoal rules, tiny registration labels and restrained shadows. Accent indicates chapter/progress/links rather than medical severity. No red alerts or faux patient monitors.

Alternatives for later visual review: cool chart paper (#EDF3F4 ground, #14292E ink, #245F82 accent, white matte panels); night desk (#142429 ground, #F1F2EB ink, #78C6B8 accent, pale paper panels). These are styling options for the same concept, not additional concepts. Warm paper is selected under delegated judgment; do not add a palette switch to the public site.

Two typefaces: Source Sans 3 for navigation/body text; IBM Plex Sans for form headings and panel printing. Both have a practical document character. Self-host licensed font files with system sans fallbacks. Desktop titles roughly 48–72px, phone 32–40px; body 18px desktop/16–18px phone; line length about 60–70 characters. Use weight, spacing and rules rather than tiny uppercase labels. Verify color contrast during build.

## Other site needs

Build means a future implementation requirement, not authorization to implement now.

| Need | Build, later or never | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Page navigation | Build: chapter rail/menu, skip links, contact access | Assistant under F10 |
| Page per project | Later: only if evidence warrants an independent shareable case study; inline detail initially | Assistant |
| Every project listed | Build: approved work index/detail at Background/Assessment; only two grounded projects initially. Others later when confirmed | Assistant |
| Contact and CV | Build when verified address and approved PDF exist; no fake destination | Assistant; Aoife supplies facts |
| Testimonials | Later, only with approved quote and attribution | Assistant |
| Languages | Build English; others later if requested | Assistant |
| Share preview and icon | Build: name/formal role, privacy-safe document illustration; five-field monogram icon, no hospital logo | Assistant, constrained by F05/F06 |
| Missing-address page | Build: plain explanation and Home/Contact links | Assistant |
| Blog | Never in initial scope | Assistant |
| Chat | Never in initial scope | Assistant |
| Legal notice | Build if applicable to hosting/content/contact setup; assess Irish/EU requirements at implementation, no assumed tracking or cookie banner | Assistant |

Further implementation requirements: descriptive page title and metadata, readable social preview, canonical URL after domain choice, optimized image sizes, lazy-loaded 3D after HTML, simple low-poly panels and capped rendering resolution. Target LCP ≤2.5s, CLS ≤0.1 and INP ≤200ms, then validate on a mid-range phone; these are future acceptance targets, not measured results. No third-party analytics assumed. Test keyboard access, reduced motion and JS/WebGL fallbacks before launch. Do not include patient material in bundles or hidden assets.

## Approval

Approve this script or identify changes. Choice of concept/look/order was delegated and recorded in decided-for-you.md. Script approval does not authorize building or publication. After approval, finalize the planning handover; this skill version stops at planning.

item.text:
I’d make the site **a handover to your next clinical informatics employer**. ISBAR gives it a structure that belongs to your working life and connects directly to the redesign you led.

The question carrying the page is: **How can nursing experience make clinical systems work better on a ward?**

I considered the audit cycle and care plan as alternatives. ISBAR wins because its headings are confirmed, familiar, and broad enough to carry both your handover work and your observation study. I’ve selected it using the judgment you delegated.

### The object and the scroll

Five paper panels—one per ISBAR field—form a single handover document. They stay with the visitor throughout the page, separating to expose evidence and coming together at the end. The panels are designed portfolio graphics; actual empty handover sheets become evidence when supplied.

| Chapter | What it shows | What happens as you scroll |
|---|---|---|
| **Identify** | Your name, **CNM1**, and **Nursing Informatics Link Nurse, one day a week**. Immediate proof: you led a five-person handover redesign group. | The five fields assemble into a readable document. Your identity and evidence appear immediately, without an opening loading sequence. |
| **Situation** | Your aim to work full time in clinical informatics, for hospitals or system vendors. Your daily working forms establish the context. | Two panels advance to connect your present role with your intended next role; the others remain visible behind them. |
| **Background** | Your career context and the ISBAR redesign. Empty old/new sheets can show the actual changes. | The panels extend into a short career line, then face the reader as a document comparison. Differences are annotated only after inspecting the sheets. |
| **Assessment** | Your forty hours of observation, identification of three workarounds, and contribution to relocating scanners. | The same panels become an observation → findings → action diagram. Movement explains the relationship between the evidence and the change. |
| **Recommendation** | A concise account of your contribution, clear ward-team attribution, and an invitation to discuss a full-time role. | The panels reunite into a complete handover. The scene settles so visitors can read, contact you and download your CV. |

The desktop sequence would take roughly ten screens, with navigation allowing visitors to jump directly to evidence or contact. Someone spending thirty seconds should still get your name, formal roles, one credible contribution and a way to reach you.

### Colours and type

My choice is **warm paper, dark ink and restrained teal**:

- Background: `#F4F1E9`
- Text: `#172A2D`
- Accent: `#006B64`
- Panels: `#FFFEF8`, with fine rules and shallow shadows

Use **Source Sans 3** for body text and navigation, and **IBM Plex Sans** for the printed document fields. Generous spacing and readable headings give the form presence. Teal marks links and progress; it doesn’t imitate clinical alerts.

The detailed plan also records cool chart-paper and night-desk alternatives, should you want a different mood.

### On a phone

The story becomes a single-column sequence with a compact document illustration above each section. Panel movements are brief; there is no long pinned scene or horizontal scrolling. Contact stays easy to find.

All content lives in ordinary HTML. Reduced-motion visitors receive static diagrams; devices without WebGL or JavaScript receive the same evidence, navigation and contact links. Nothing essential depends on reading text inside 3D.

### What else it needs

The initial site should include chapter navigation, accessible evidence details, a verified contact link, an approved downloadable CV, a social-sharing preview, a document-derived icon and a useful missing-page screen. It should load the text before the 3D.

I’d keep it English-only initially, with additional project pages and testimonials added when there is approved material to support them. A blog and chat are outside the initial scope.

I have **omitted the near-miss story entirely**, excluded the whiteboard photo and hospital logo, and kept the scanning improvement attributed to the ward team. The numerical result stays out of final copy until its exact measure and period are clear. I haven’t assumed MSc completion, poster permissions, a contact address or further employer permissions.

The complete script is in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-nurse-with-Ivo8GY/docs/story/storyboard.md), with the [three concepts](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-nurse-with-Ivo8GY/docs/story/concepts.md) and [delegated decisions](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-nurse-with-Ivo8GY/docs/story/decided-for-you.md) alongside it. **Nothing has been built.**

Does this storyboard have your approval, or what would you change?

The [storyfolio skill](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-nurse-with-Ivo8GY/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) ends when “the person has said yes to a storyboard.” This approval completes the planning stage; it does not authorize building.
